nameStory: The "horned" in Horned Beakrush comes from the tiny pointed projections on its seeds that look like miniature horns. The "beak" part refers to the bird-like pointed tip of these same seeds, while "rush" is a bit of a misnomer since this plant is actually a sedge, not a true rush.
description: Horned Beakrush is a delicate, grass-like sedge that forms small clumps in wet areas. This petite perennial grows only 4 to 16 inches tall, making it easy to overlook among taller wetland plants. Its stems are topped with just a few small, narrow brown flower clusters that look almost thread-like. The whole plant has an airy, delicate appearance that sets it apart from burlier wetland sedges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat little clumps of very thin stems, much more delicate and wispy than most other sedges you'll encounter

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely narrow, almost hair-like leaves that feel smooth between your fingers - much thinner than grass blades

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Only 1-4 small brown spikelets per stem, each about the size of a grain of rice, creating a sparse, delicate flower head

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds with distinctive beak-like tips and small horn-like projections that you can see with a hand lens

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Stays quite short at 4-16 inches tall, making it one of the smaller sedges in New England wetlands

habitat: Look for Horned Beakrush in calcium-rich wetlands like fens, wet meadows, and along sandy or rocky lakeshores and pond edges. It prefers areas with neutral to alkaline water rather than acidic bogs. You'll often find it in the transition zones between open water and upland areas, sometimes growing on wet limestone ledges or in calcareous seeps.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge as tiny tufts of thread-like green growth, easily missed among other emerging wetland plants.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from mid to late summer, producing the small brown spikelets that help distinguish it from other sedges. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the distinctive beaked fruits become visible, while the plant begins to turn brown and becomes less noticeable.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Despite being found across a huge range from Labrador to Texas, Horned Beakrush has only been spotted 6 times in all of New England, making it one of our rarest sedges - you're more likely to see a moose than find this tiny plant!
confusionNotes: Its delicate, thread-like appearance might remind you of fine grasses, but remember "sedges have edges" - roll the stem between your fingers and you'll feel the triangular cross-section that all sedges have. The sparse, few-flowered clusters also help separate it from denser-flowered grasses.
contextualKnowledge: Like many sedges, this species is often called a "rush" in its common name, which can be confusing since true rushes belong to a different plant family entirely. The sedge family (which includes this species) typically has triangular stems and closed leaf sheaths, while true rushes have round stems.
compareHints: Horned Beakrush is much more delicate and shorter than its beakrush relatives like White Beak-sedge or Brown Beakrush. While other beakrushes tend to be taller and more robust with denser flower clusters, Horned Beakrush maintains its wispy, thread-like character and sparse flowering pattern. Its preference for calcareous wetlands also sets it apart from some relatives that prefer acidic conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its beaksedge relatives, white beak-sedge is the only one with distinctly white or pale cream flower clusters - the others like brown beakrush and brownish beaked-rush have darker, brownish flower heads.
Among New England's beaksedges, brownish beaked-rush is distinguished by its compact, bead-like brown flower clusters, while white beak-sedge has whitish flowers and tall beakrush grows much larger.
Among New England's beakrushes, Tall Beakrush stands out for its robust size and sturdy growth habit - it's the linebacker of the beakrush family.
Among New England's beakrush species, Brown Beakrush is distinguished by its consistently brown flower clusters and relatively small stature.
Among New England's beaksedges, narrowfruit horned beaksedge stands out for its exceptionally slender fruits and sparse growth habit.
Torrey's beaksedge is much smaller and more delicate than its relatives like white beak-sedge, which forms larger, more obvious clumps.
Among its beaksedge relatives, Long-beaked Bald-rush stands out for having the longest, most prominent seed beaks and the sparsest flower clusters.
